summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework: the constitutional and criminal prohibitions on discrimination and hate crimes on gender-identity grounds, legal gender recognition without surgery, same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348 and 366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.

Bahia carries a high trans homicide burden by raw count. The ANTRA 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in the state during 2025, behind the leading states at 8, and across the 1,261 killings documented nationally between 2017 and 2025 Bahia ranks third by raw count with 97, after São Paulo with 151 and Ceará with 107; Valor Internacional's state-level breakdown for 2025 places Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair. A 2022 ANTRA dossier ranked Bahia seventh in the country that year, with 7 killings of travestis in the state.

Police in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in western Bahia, are investigating the killing of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, as a feminicide. She was choked to death over the weekend of 6-7 December 2025; the suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove her body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and asserting self-defence, and the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide line of inquiry.

State-level protection exists in Bahia's own law. The Legislative Assembly passed the Millena Passos Law on 1 June 2022, banning discrimination on the ground of gender identity, signed on 30 June 2022 by Assembly President Adolfo Menezes and named for the trans activist Millena Passos; a parallel bill banning discrimination on sexual orientation was passed and signed on the same dates. Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997.

Documents and public administration follow state rules of their own. Transgender people in Bahia have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018. On 23 May 2017 Governor Rui Costa decreed that travesti and transsexual persons may use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across all organs of the state's direct and indirect public administration, with the social name required to appear alongside the legal name on official documents and guardian authorisation needed for minors. On 11 May 2022 the Court of Justice of the State of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents.

Salvador, the state capital, moved in the opposite direction on schools: the City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools on 17 December 2025, signed into law by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis on 26 March 2026, and the municipal law now prohibits gender-identity material in Salvador's schools.

Partner and family recognition is documented locally. Notaries in Bahia have recognised same-sex marriages since 26 November 2012, the stable-union book is recognised by the National Institute of Social Security for inheritance and pension purposes with 30 reported legal cases in the state including a surviving same-sex spouse's pension, and on 9 March 2010 a Salvador court authorised adoption by a lesbian couple.
tangentialFactors:
The raw-count rankings above are not per-capita. ANTRA's dossier counts killings nationally, and Bahia's third place with 97 killings over nine years reflects its population alongside its risk; the same applies to the 2025 count of 7, which trails states recording 8. A state's position in this table should not be read as a measure of danger relative to smaller states.

Bahia appears in the top band of consecutive annual ANTRA dossiers, seventh in 2022 and third cumulatively through 2025, which grounds a persistence finding rather than a single bad year. Pernambuco led the 2022 ranking nationally, not Bahia.

Documented homophobic violence in the state includes a 2022 attack on a teenager in Camaçari that drew national repercussions and mobilised state authorities, and Grupo Gay da Bahia's 2004 list naming 159 murdered LGBTQ people that year, some deaths attributed directly to homophobia. In 2008 the travesti club dancer Léo Kret won a Salvador city council seat with 12,861 votes and on taking office insisted on a feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom, defying the chamber's dress-code norms.

The national debate over anti-discrimination legislation and the identification of religious institutions as sources of rising intolerance play out over state politics as well; Bahia's own legislative protections were passed by the same Assembly that has since considered restrictions on gender-identity teaching.
localsOnly:
On 26 December 2024 Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues sanctioned Law 14,806, which exempts the cost of protest certificates so that document rectification is free of charge for transgender people in Bahia.

The Bahia Public Defender's Office works with other agencies on joint efforts to facilitate document rectification for trans residents, including the social-name process established by the 2017 decree and the third gender option opened by the Court of Justice in 2022.

A preventative STD and AIDS programme for transvestite sex workers in Bahia produced a booklet, folder and poster in realistic language and images, ran weekly safe-sex workshops and outreach, and recorded 900 interventions and distribution of 14,400 condoms in six months.

Conjugal visitation with same-sex partners has been available in all Brazilian jails since February 2015 under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council, and the national prison framework gives LGBTQ prisoners a separate place, address by social name rather than birth name, placement in women's prisons by gender identity, and the choice of male or female clothing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bahia-specific trans-prisoner placement rule, special unit, segregation practice, or documented case was identified in the sources; no detail is given for the Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária da Bahia. The national custody framework applies, but whether Bahia's prison system operates LGBTI-specific living spaces is unresolved.

The ANTRA killing counts are reported as raw totals. The sources provide no per-capita or population-adjusted figures for Bahia, and the underlying methodology is contested: critics describe the counting of all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people irrespective of motive as unscientific, and note that interstate and international comparisons are distorted by differences in documentation capacity. The 2025 and cumulative rankings therefore rest on an unresolved methodological question.

No enforcement record for the Millena Passos Law was sourced: the inventory contains no reported prosecution, penalty or administrative action brought under it since 2022.

Access to gender-affirming care within Bahia's own state health facilities, waiting times, and the availability of surgery outside the federal university-hospital network are not documented in these sources.

The status of the Salvador school ordinance after its March 2026 enactment, including any legal challenge by state or federal authorities, is unresolved in the sources.
